cards.title: Graham Cormode and S. Muthukrishnan
cards.prompt: Count-Min gives up exactness on purpose. Name the one thing its authors refused to give up with it, and say what that refusal bought them that every earlier sketch lacked.
cards.answer: The sign of the error. They kept it one-sided — an estimate lands at or above the truth, never below — where all previous sketch constructions had two-sided error. That is what converts a probabilistic heavy-hitter answer into one where no true heavy hitter can ever be missed, and it is why a top-K list built on a sketch is safe to act on.
cards.body: Cormode was a DIMACS postdoctoral fellow; Muthukrishnan is listed on the report at Rutgers University and AT&T Research. Their June 2003 tech report traded exact counts for a fixed array, then spent its novelty claim not on the space saving but on the direction of the error.

cards.title: The AT&T backbone that could not be counted
cards.prompt: Gigascope's paper prices AT&T's backbone in two units at once. Give both numbers, and say which of the two is the one that rules out an exact per-flow hash map.
cards.answer: 500 Gbytes of data per day, and about ten billion fifty-byte records per day — and both figures are for already-sampled, already-aggregated router traffic summaries, not raw packets. The record count is the one that kills the map: an exact counter costs memory per distinct key, so the bill scales with how many distinct flows appear — and the records they hide in arrive ten billion a day.
cards.body: Chuck Cranor, Theodore Johnson, Oliver Spatscheck and Vladislav Shkapenyuk, SIGMOD 2003. Gigascope answered SQL-like queries over live network streams: seven installations, the largest peaking at 1.2 million packets per second on an inexpensive dual 2.4 GHz CPU server, and running three months nonstop. Further deployments across AT&T, including OC48, were still in negotiations.

cards.title: DIMACS Technical Report 2003-20
cards.prompt: Cite the Count-Min sketch properly to an interviewer: give the archival journal, volume, pages and year — then name the earlier document that stated the sketch's point-query theorem nearly two years before it.
cards.answer: Journal of Algorithms, volume 55, issue 1, pages 58-75, April 2005. The earlier document is DIMACS Technical Report 2003-20, dated June 2003, which already states Theorem 1: a_i is at most a-hat_i, and with probability 1 minus delta, a-hat_i is at most a_i plus epsilon times the L1 norm of a. The tech report predates the journal's print date by nearly two years — which is why the sketch is dated 2003, 2004 and 2005 in different bibliographies.
cards.body: Titled "Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications", June 2003. Named for its two operations: counting first, computing the minimum next. The archival version is Journal of Algorithms 55(1):58-75, April 2005 — so a paper everyone calls recent is older than most of the systems that use it.

cards.title: One-sided error is why display can be approximate
cards.sub: 2003 · the asymmetry every trending stack inherits
cards.prompt: Suppose the 2003 authors had settled for the two-sided error of the sketches before them. Name two things in this chapter's design that would stop working, and say why.
cards.answer: First, the top-K guarantee: with two-sided error an estimate can land below the truth, so a real winner can be pushed out of the list, and 'the error only promotes impostors, never demotes a winner' is simply false. Second, the whole safety argument at the rank-K boundary: the published list is no longer a superset of the true heavy hitters, so comparing the gap at rank K against the error bound stops settling the question, and candidate-generation-then-re-query loses its soundness.
cards.body: The report claims the one-sided bound as its advance over every earlier construction, then cashes it in at once: previous sketch methods gave probabilistic guarantees about outputting heavy hitters, and theirs gives certainty. Every trending and telemetry stack since inherits that asymmetry — the display path may approximate, because the approximation only ever adds.
